source.title: AdaBatch: Adaptive Batch Sizes for Training Deep Neural Networks
source.authors: Aditya Devarakonda; Maxim Naumov; Michael Garland

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied; no apparent truncation or document mismatch.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether changing batch size during training affects held-out test error, using adaptive schedules and fixed-batch comparisons rather than the fixed-epoch large-batch comparison in V5.
record.gate_note: Reports test-error results for adaptive and fixed batch-size training, which bear on V5. It does not test random-label memorization, width beyond interpolation, architecture comparisons, optimizer generalization, dropout, sharpness measures, or memorized-example removal. Cited findings about prior work are not extracted as rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures held-out error under fixed and increasing batch sizes at common epoch budgets: 100 epochs on CIFAR and 90 on ImageNet. Its fixed-batch comparisons test V5's penalty, and its adaptive schedules test V5's recipe-dependent recovery. It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially correct. The authors conclude that scheduled batch increases preserve approximately the test accuracy of smaller fixed batches while improving CIFAR runtime, with measured speedups up to 6.25×. They report ImageNet effective batches up to 524288 with similar test error under suitable schedules, but do not measure ImageNet speedups because training uses gradient accumulation. Section 4.2 gives a less-than-2% error-difference bound for the maximum-speedup comparison, although the abstract and conclusion summarize less than 1%.
record.recipe_differences: The study changes batch size during training and compares test errors with fixed-batch schedules; it does not test the original claim's random-label memorization or generalization setup.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset, initial batch size, batch-size increase factor, learning-rate warmup and decay schedule affect test-error convergence. In particular, an 8× increase performs poorly when starting at 16384, while it is similar in final error when starting at 8192.
record.problems: Test-error comparisons are mainly described from figures without exact values in the text; several summaries use relative differences without specifying whether these are percentage points or relative percentages. Five-trial means are reported for some experiments, but uncertainty is not stated for most ImageNet comparisons.
record.rows_left_out: No test-error conditions from the described text were omitted; exact values only displayed in figures are not reconstructed.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its coexistence with natural-label generalization.
Width beyond interpolation and held-out error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under different tuning budgets.

Language models; recovery through longer training or normalization and regularization changes. ImageNet adaptive schedules are compared with their initial large batch, not with a trained batch-256 baseline.
Effects of adding or removing dropout and weight decay.
Measured magnitude-aware sharpness and its association with generalization gaps.
Removing memorized examples versus random examples.

missing.what: Direct fixed-large versus fixed-small CIFAR test-error comparisons. Section 4.1 states adaptive errors are significantly below the largest fixed batches while near the smallest; the timing discussion also explicitly excludes largest batches because their test errors are not comparable. Existing CIFAR rows record only adaptive-versus-small outcomes.
missing.locator: Section 4.1, Figures 1–2 and discussion following Table 1

missing.what: VGG19 BN and ResNet-20 adaptive 1024–16384 versus fixed 1024, both with warmup: the text reports similar test errors with less than 1% difference. R7–R8 instead compare against fixed 128, and R9–R10 cover only adaptive 128–2048.

record.verdict_notes: Observed states for successful adaptive schedules refer to V5's explicit adaptation clause. Near-equality under an adapted recipe therefore supports that clause rather than challenging the fixed-recipe penalty. Exact figure values are unavailable in the supplied text; percent differences should not be silently converted to percentage points. R11–R13 and R15 need separate rows for their distinct conditions.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fit and natural-label generalization coexistence.

The study does not compare fixed batch sizes at a common epoch budget as the main intervention; it examines adaptive schedules, including adaptive versus fixed settings. It does not test language models.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relationship to the train-test gap.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring test accuracy.

rows.baseline: Smallest fixed batch size (256); numerical test error not stated in text.
rows.value: Adaptive batch size; mean test error within 1% of the smallest fixed batch size.
rows.uncertainty: Mean ± standard deviation over 5 trials, numerical values not stated in text.

rows.check: The reported near-preservation of test error supports V5's adaptation clause; 'partial' does not follow simply from a within-1% bound. Record the adaptive learning-rate multiplier 0.75 versus fixed-batch 0.375 every 20 epochs.

rows.subject: VGG19 with Batch Normalization
rows.operation_detail: Compared adaptive 1024–16384 with fixed batch size 128 on CIFAR-100, with gradual learning-rate scaling.
rows.measure: Test error difference versus fixed batch-size 128.
rows.baseline: Fixed batch size 128; exact test error not stated in text.
rows.value: Less than 2% difference in test error; adaptive schedule average speedup 3.54× over 5 trials.
rows.uncertainty: Average speedup over 5 trials; test-error uncertainty not stated.
rows.note: The stated comparison includes speedup, but the row records the test-error outcome relevant to V5.
rows.check: A less-than-2% difference without its direction or an unadapted comparator cannot establish a residual penalty or its reduction. Keep the bound, but do not infer incomplete recovery from it. The Section 4.2 baseline learning rate is 0.1, decayed by 0.25; adaptive training doubles batches and multiplies learning rate by 0.5 every 20 epochs.

rows.subject: ResNet-50
rows.operation_detail: Compared adaptive batch size starting at 4096 with fixed batch sizes on ImageNet.
rows.baseline: Fixed batch size 4096; numerical test error not stated in text.
rows.value: Adaptive convergence closely matches fixed batch size 4096; fixed 8192 and 16,384 do not converge to the test errors of fixed 4096 and AdaBatch.
rows.note: The result supports adaptive performance near a smaller-batch reference and reports poorer convergence for fixed larger batches; exact values are figure-only.
rows.check: This row combines two results that should be separated: fixed 8192 and 16384 batches have worse test error than fixed 4096, while adaptive 4096–16384 matches fixed 4096. Adaptive learning rate is multiplied by 0.2 every 30 epochs, versus 0.1 for fixed batches.

source_check.correct: Starting learning rate: 0.1. Fixed-batch learning-rate multiplier: 0.1 every 30 epochs. Adaptive learning-rate multiplier: 0.2 with batch doubling every 30 epochs. Adaptive 4096–16384 matches fixed 4096; larger fixed batches have worse test error.
source_check.problem: The condition gives the fixed-batch learning-rate decay without distinguishing the adaptive schedule's different multiplier.

rows.subject: ResNet-50
rows.operation_detail: Compared adaptive batch-size increase factors on ImageNet with warmup, starting at 8192.
rows.measure: Test-error curves and final test error.
rows.baseline: Fixed batch size 8192; numerical test error not stated in text.
rows.value: Adaptive curves closely match the fixed-batch curve; with 8× increase convergence slows after Epoch 60, but final test error is similar.
rows.note: The convergence slowdown is explicitly stated; numerical errors are figure-only.
rows.check: All three schedules retain similar final test error at 90 epochs, supporting the adaptation clause. The 8× schedule's temporary slowdown does not establish a final-error penalty. Its final effective batch is 524288.

rows.subject: ResNet-50
rows.operation_detail: Compared adaptive batch-size increase factors on ImageNet with warmup, starting at 16384.
rows.baseline: Adaptive schedules with 2× and 4× increase; exact test error not stated.
rows.value: Increasing batch size by 8× results in poor convergence; the text attributes this to increasing it too much and too early. A 4× increase does not significantly alter final test error and attains final batch size 262,144.
rows.note: Condition-dependent result: 8× increase gives poor convergence from this starting batch size, while 4× is reported not to significantly alter final error.
rows.check: Split this mixed row: 4× increases preserve final test error at final batch 262144, whereas 8× increases produce poor convergence. The successful and unsuccessful schedules require separate states and condition-specific verdicts.

source_check.correct: Separate conditions: starting batch 16384 with 4× increases preserves final test error at final batch 262144, state observed for adaptive preservation; 8× increases produce poor convergence, state absent for adaptive preservation. Exact test errors are not stated.
source_check.problem: One partial state conflates successful preservation with an explicitly unsuccessful schedule; the text does not establish partial recovery for the 8× schedule.
